slides.title: What are Vector Databases?
content: Converts query to vector, uses HNSW to find closest chunks.
slides.narration:
We have learned about the science of HNSW.
Now, let us explore the tools that implement it.
We store our meaning coordinates, or vectors, in a Vector Database.
Think of it as a highly optimized address book for vectors.
When you get a new query, the database converts it into a vector.
It then uses its internal HNSW algorithm.
This instantly finds the closest vectors, which are our data chunks.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a vector database as an 'address book' with vectors flowing in and out, connected by HNSW graph.

slides.title: Choosing Your Vector Library
slides.narration:
You have three main choices for your vector library tool.
Let us look at each type.
slides.image_prompt: Decision tree or flowchart showing three paths for choosing a vector library.

slides.title: In-Memory Libraries: FAISS
content: What it is: Code library (Meta) in Python script.
Pros: Blazing fast, good for research/prototyping, millions of vectors.
Cons: No persistence, no APIs, limited filtering.
slides.narration:
First, we have In-Memory Libraries, like FAISS.
FAISS is a code library from Meta.
It runs directly within your Python script.
Its main advantage is blazing speed.
It is perfect for research, prototyping, and smaller projects.
It can handle up to a few million vectors.
However, it is not a full database.
It does not handle data persistence, APIs, or complex filtering well.
slides.image_prompt: Icon for a Python script with a fast-forward symbol, representing FAISS.

slides.title: Open-Source Databases
content: What it is: Standalone database program on a server (Chroma, Weaviate, Qdrant).
Pros: Powerful, billions of vectors, metadata filtering, free.
Cons: Requires self-management, scaling, and maintenance.
slides.narration:
Next, consider Open-Source Databases.
Examples include Chroma, Weaviate, and Qdrant.
These are full, standalone database programs.
You run them on a server.
They offer the best of both worlds.
They are powerful and can handle billions of vectors.
They also support metadata filtering, and are free.
The main drawback is you must manage, scale, and maintain the server yourself.
slides.image_prompt: Icons representing Chroma, Weaviate, and Qdrant around a server rack icon.

slides.title: Managed Services
content: What it is: Serverless cloud database (Pinecone).
Pros: Infinitely scalable, zero maintenance, easy to use.
Cons: Can be expensive, data lives on third-party servers.
slides.narration:
Finally, we have Managed Services, like Pinecone.
These are serverless databases in the cloud.
You pay a provider to handle everything.
The pros include infinite scalability and zero maintenance.
They are very easy to use.
The cons are that they can be expensive.
Also, your data lives on someone else's server.
slides.image_prompt: Cloud icon with a dollar sign, representing managed services like Pinecone.

slides.title: Why We Use FAISS
content: Parameters: d (vector dimension), M (neighbors per node), efSearch (accuracy/speed).
slides.narration:
For our hands-on work, we will start with FAISS.
This allows you to directly interact with HNSW parameters.
These include 'd' for vector dimension.
'M' for the number of neighbors per node.
And 'efSearch' for the search-time accuracy and speed trade-off.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of FAISS logo with HNSW graph parameters (d, M, efSearch) highlighted.

slides.title: Setting up Python Environment
slides.narration:
Let us set up our Python environment.
Step 1: Open your terminal or command prompt.
Step 2: Create a new directory for this project.
Type mkdir vector_db_tutorial and press Enter.
Step 3: Navigate into the new directory.
Type cd vector_db_tutorial and press Enter.
Step 4: Create a virtual environment.
Type python3 -m venv venv and press Enter.
Step 5: Activate the virtual environment.
Type source venv/bin/activate for Linux and macOS.
For Windows, type .\venv\Scripts\activate.
Then press Enter.
You should see (venv) at the start of your prompt.

slides.video_prompt: Demonstration of opening a terminal, creating a directory, navigating into it, creating a virtual environment, and activating it.

slides.title: Installing FAISS
content: Install faiss-cpu and numpy using pip.
slides.narration:
Now, let us install the FAISS library.
Step 1: Ensure your virtual environment is active.
Step 2: Install faiss-cpu using pip.
Type pip install faiss-cpu numpy and press Enter.
Step 3: Wait for the installation to complete.
Step 4: Verify the installation.
Type pip show faiss-cpu and press Enter.
You should see details about the installed package.
slides.image_prompt: Screenshot of a terminal showing 'pip install faiss-cpu numpy' and 'pip show faiss-cpu' commands and their outputs.
slides.video_prompt: Demonstration of installing faiss-cpu and numpy within the activated virtual environment, then verifying the installation with 'pip show'.

slides.title: Verifying FAISS Installation
slides.narration:
Let us quickly verify that FAISS is working.
Step 1: Open a Python interpreter in your terminal.
Type python and press Enter.
Step 2: Try to import faiss.
Type import faiss and press Enter.
If no error appears, FAISS is correctly installed.
Step 3: Exit the Python interpreter.
Type exit() and press Enter.
Pause the video and try this yourself.
